question: Linda finds an old, broken version of the report with Sarah's name on it. What's going on here?

options.text: The conclusion went straight to his competence rather than to what happened to the file
options.note: A file on a shared drive got replaced. That has a dozen boring explanations. The one that got picked first was that he isn't good enough.

options.text: Nobody asked him for his account before deciding what had happened
options.note: He isn't a witness to his own work. The version history was one click away and no one opened it.

options.text: "Don't let me down again" turns one incident into a pattern he now has to disprove
options.note: "Again" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. From here he's not starting from neutral, he's starting from behind.

options.text: Sarah deliberately sabotaged him and that's the real problem
options.note: She might have. We never find out, and it changes less than you'd think — if nobody checks either way, the outcome is the same for him.

options.text: He should have kept his own copy instead of trusting the shared drive
options.note: Reasonable habit. Notice that it's a habit only he needs, and that it's being suggested after the fact as though the gap were his.

options.text: It would have been better handled in a meeting room instead of at his desk
options.note: The audience made it worse. The assumption underneath it would have been identical behind a closed door.

question: He's asked to stay back and clean the kitchenette, and later Jean asks what she gets in return for helping him. What's the problem?

options.text: He was picked for the cleaning because of assumptions about him, not because it was his turn
options.note: "You seem like you'd be good at it" isn't a rota. It's a category, and he's been put in it.

options.text: "You clean up so well" makes his appearance the joke in a work setting
options.note: The line works twice, and both meanings are about how he looks. Neither is about the report he spent three weeks on.

options.text: Jean turned ordinary collegial help into something he has to pay for
options.note: Everyone else gets a hand with a bug for free. Pricing it — even as a joke — makes him ask himself what the currency is.

options.text: Someone has to clean the kitchenette and it may as well be him
options.note: Someone does. Track who it is over a month, and that's the whole point.

options.text: Jean was obviously joking and he read too much into it
options.note: She might have been. He still has to decide, in the moment, which reading to act on — and he'll wear it if he guesses wrong.

options.text: He should have just said no to the kitchenette
options.note: On the day his competence was publicly questioned. Consider what saying no would have cost him that afternoon.

question: Several people watched this day happen. Where could someone have stepped in?

options.text: At the surrounding desks, after Linda walked off
options.note: Nobody looked up. Not during, which is hard — but not after either, which isn't. "That didn't look like your file" would have cost nothing.

options.text: In the thread, by replying to his answer or pointing back to it
options.note: The cheapest bystander action in the building. "This is answered above" takes four seconds and makes him visible again.

options.text: In the meeting, by volunteering before the silence did its work
options.note: The silence is the mechanism. Anyone could have broken it, and the person who breaks it barely pays anything.

options.text: By reporting Linda to HR on his behalf
options.note: It skips him again — the second time in one day someone else decides what happens to him without asking.

options.text: By taking him aside afterwards and telling him to let it roll off
options.note: This is offered as kindness and lands as instruction. It tells him the problem is how he's taking it.

options.text: Nothing — none of it was directed at anyone else, so it wasn't their business
options.note: Everyone in the room is part of what the room is like. Sitting it out is a contribution too.

question: Someone wants to check in with him at the end of this day. What actually helps?

options.text: Believing his account of the file without making him prove it first
options.note: He's spent all day being disbelieved. Starting from belief is the whole difference between support and another interrogation.

options.text: Asking what he wants to happen next instead of deciding for him
options.note: Every decision today got made over his head. This is the one that doesn't have to be.

options.text: Naming the pattern across the day rather than treating each thing separately
options.note: Any one of these is survivable and deniable. Together they're a day. Someone else seeing that shape is enormously relieving.

options.text: Telling him to document everything from now on
options.note: Practical, and it's a second job. It asks him to keep evidence on his own workplace, forever, in case he needs it — which is its own kind of weight.

options.text: Offering to have a word with Linda for him
options.note: Generous, and still someone else steering. Ask first — he may want exactly this, and he may not.

options.text: Reassuring him that Sarah almost certainly didn't mean it
options.note: It might be true. It's also an argument about intent when what he needs acknowledged is effect.
